title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #05
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #05 · Q1
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Concept) — List II (Thinker)
A. "Bricolage" — I. Martin Heidegger
B. "Dasein" — II. Sigmund Freud
C. "Parapraxes" — III. Levi-Strauss
D. "Polyphony" — IV. Mikhail Bakhtin

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A - III, B - I, C - II, D - IV
A - I, B - II, C - III, D - IV
A - II, B - I, C - III, D - IV
A - IV, B - I, C - II, D - III
items.explanation: Claude Lévi-Strauss introduced 'bricolage' in The Savage Mind (1962, A-III), Martin Heidegger analyzed 'Dasein' (being-there) in Being and Time (1927, B-I), Sigmund Freud studied 'parapraxes' (Freudian slips) in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901, C-II), and Mikhail Bakhtin theorized 'polyphony' in Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics (1929, D-IV).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q2
items.stem: Langston Hughes’ poem “I too Sing America” is a response to which of the following poets?
items.explanation: Langston Hughes composed "I, Too" ("I, too, sing America") in 1926 as a direct dialogue with and critique of Walt Whitman's patriotic anthem "I Hear America Singing" (1860). Hughes asserts that African Americans are an integral, beautiful, and equal part of the American nation who claim their rightful place at the table.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q3
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true about Reader Response Criticism?
A. It challenges the notion that the meaning is located within the text.
B. It refutes that the author is the originator of meaning.
C. It sees the reader as a source of meaning.
D. It treats the text as self-sufficient.
E. It appreciates the texts that are historical.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Reader-response criticism rejects the New Critical view of the text as a self-sufficient container of meaning (A) as well as authorial intentionalism (B), positioning the reader as an active producer of meaning (C); NTA awarded credit for Options 1, 2, and 3.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q4
items.stem: Who among the ancients prescribed that poetry should both instruct and delight ?
items.explanation: Horace in the Ars Poetica said poets aim 'to instruct or to delight, or to combine both' (utile et dulce).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q5
items.stem:
Arrange the works in chronological sequence:
A. Structuralist Poetics
B. Course in General Linguistics
C. The Pursuit of Signs
D. The Pleasure of the Text
E. The Implied Reader
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological publication sequence is: Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (1916, B), Roland Barthes's The Pleasure of the Text (1973, D), Wolfgang Iser's The Implied Reader (1974 English translation, E), Jonathan Culler's Structuralist Poetics (1975, A), and Culler's The Pursuit of Signs (1981, C), giving B, D, E, A, C.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q6
items.stem:
Which of the following is not a part of the series of poems called Jejuri, written by Arun
Kolatkar ?
items.explanation: Arun Kolatkar's Commonwealth Poetry Prize-winning sequence Jejuri (1976) includes the poems 'The Priest', 'Chaitanya', and 'Yeshwant Rao', as well as the famous poem 'An Old Woman', but there is no poem titled 'Old Man' in the volume.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q7
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as
Reason R

Assertion A: Signs are never neutral or innocent.

Reason R: In all cases signs are organized into systems that convey some meaning.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Ais false but R is true
items.explanation: In semiotic and cultural theory (such as Roland Barthes's Mythologies), linguistic and cultural signs are never ideologically neutral or innocent. This is because signs never exist in isolation; they are always organized into coded sign systems and cultural conventions designed to construct and convey specific meanings.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q8
items.stem: Which of the following works is reviewed in George Orwell's essay, Inside the Whale?
items.explanation: Orwell's 'Inside the Whale' (1940) is a long review-essay on Henry Miller's novel 'Tropic of Cancer'.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q9
items.stem:
Identify the correct combination among the following :
A. Demons — Novel
B. Landlady — Novella
C. The Crocodile — Short-Story
D. A Writer's Diary — Essay
E. Mary Stuart — Translation
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Among Fyodor Dostoevsky's works, The Landlady (1847) is a novella (B), 'The Crocodile' (1865) is a satirical short story (C), and A Writer's Diary (1873–1881) consists of journalistic essays and sketches (D), giving Option 4 (B, C and D only).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q10
items.stem: The first scene in Girish Karnad’s Tughlaq opens in front of a …………..
items.explanation: Scene 1 of Girish Karnad's historical drama Tughlaq (1964) opens outside the royal court of justice in Delhi, where citizens gather to discuss Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq's administration and witness the outcome of a Brahmin's lawsuit against the crown.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q11
items.stem:
Match List - I with List - II.
List - I | List - II
(A) Untouchable | (I) Raja Rao
(B) Serpent and the Rope | (II) R. K. Narayan
(C) Nectar in a Sieve | (III) Mulk Raj Anand
(D) A Tiger for Malgudi | (IV) Kamala Markandeya
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Indian English novels match their authors as follows: Untouchable (1935) by Mulk Raj Anand (A-III), The Serpent and the Rope (1960) by Raja Rao (B-I), Nectar in a Sieve (1954) by Kamala Markandaya (C-IV), and A Tiger for Malgudi (1983) by R. K. Narayan (D-II).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q12
items.stem: Who described Raja Rammohun Roy as ‘the inaugurator of the modern age in India’?
items.explanation: Rabindranath Tagore described Raja Rammohun Roy as 'the inaugurator of the modern age in India' during Roy's death centenary in 1933, honoring his pioneering role in launching the Bengal Renaissance, educational modernization, and social reform.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q13
items.stem:
Which of the following authors have been correctly matched with their works?
A. Malcolm Bradbury - The History Man
B. William Golding - Rites of Passage
C. Seamus Heaney - Darkness Visible
D. Brian Friel - Dancing at Lughnasa
E. Molly Keane - The Norman Conquests

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Malcolm Bradbury wrote the campus novel The History Man (1975, A), William Golding wrote the Booker-winning sea novel Rites of Passage (1980, B), and Brian Friel wrote the play Dancing at Lughnasa (1990, D), whereas Darkness Visible is by William Golding and The Norman Conquests is by Alan Ayckbourn.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q14
items.stem: How many tales and pilgrims are there in Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales?
items.explanation: Chaucer's unfinished The Canterbury Tales contains 24 tales (including the Canon's Yeoman's Tale and two tales told by Chaucer the pilgrim: 'Tale of Sir Thopas' and 'Tale of Melibee'), matching the standard UGC-NET option '23 pilgrims and 24 tales'.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q15
items.stem: Choose the right chronological sequence below :
options: Victorian Period – Jacobean Period – Tudor Period – Restoration Period
Edwardian Period – Tudor Period – Jacobean Period – Victorian Period
Jacobean Period – Tudor Period – Restoration Period – Edwardian Period
Tudor Period – Jacobean Period – Restoration Period – Edwardian Period
items.explanation: The proper chronological succession of English literary periods is Tudor Period (1485–1603) followed by Jacobean Period (1603–1625), Restoration Period (1660–1700), and Edwardian Period (1901–1910).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q16
items.stem: Identify Petrarch's sonnet sequence from among the following
items.explanation: Fourteenth-century Italian humanist Francesco Petrarch's vernacular lyric sequence Il Canzoniere is also known by its Italian opening words, Rime sparse ("Scattered Rhymes"), and is largely addressed to his idealized beloved, Laura.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q17
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Things acquire a rational signification, and not only one of simple usage, because an other is associated with my relations with them.
Statement II: In designating a thing, I designate it to the other.
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
items.explanation: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, quoted verbatim from Emmanuel Levinas's Totality and Infinity: An Essay on Exteriority (1961), arguing that objects acquire rational linguistic signification through intersubjective relation and address to the Other.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q18
items.stem: Which of the following is not included in the positive evils of Scott as a novelist?
options: His great haste in the composition of his stories
His haphazard financial methods which tended to over production
He had sensitive ear for rhythm and melody
Haste in the construction of his plots
items.explanation: Sir Walter Scott's contemporary and later critics censured him for hasty composition, careless plotting, and excessive commercial output ('positive evils' of his novel-writing), whereas possessing a sensitive ear for rhythm and melody is an artistic virtue of his poetry and style rather than a flaw.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q19
items.stem:
In Pinter's Birthday Party Stanley is terrorised by two visitors to a seaside boarding house.
Identify the two
(a)
McGrath
(b)
Goldberg
(c)
McCann
(d)
Robinson
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In Harold Pinter's comedy of menace The Birthday Party (1957), the reclusive pianist Stanley Webber is interrogated and terrorized at Meg and Petey Boles's seaside boarding house by two sinister intruders, Nat Goldberg and Dermot McCann.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q20
items.stem:
Identify the author of the following
lines :

Let sea-discoverers to new worlds
have gone,

Let Maps to other, worlds on worlds
have shown

Let us possess one world, each hath
one, and is one
items.explanation: These lines are from John Donne's metaphysical love poem 'The Good-Morrow' (published in Songs and Sonnets, 1633), in which the speaker declares that the lovers' room contains a complete world superior to any newly discovered lands.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q21
items.stem:
Match the List-I with List-II
List I (Theatre):
A. Abbey Theatre
B. Theatre of the Absurd
C. Hope Theatre
D. Theatre of Silence

List II (Leading figure/Founder):
I. Martin Esslin
II. W.B. Yeats
III. Jean Jacques Barnard
IV. Philip Henslowe

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The theatrical movements and venues match their founders or theorists as follows: Dublin's Abbey Theatre was co-founded by W. B. Yeats in 1904 (A-II), the term 'Theatre of the Absurd' was coined by critic Martin Esslin in 1961 (B-I), London's Hope Theatre was built by impresario Philip Henslowe in 1613–14 (C-IV), and the 'Theatre of Silence' (théâtre du silence) was pioneered by French playwright Jean-Jacques Bernard in the 1920s (D-III).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q22
items.stem: What does Pierre Bourdieu imply by the term 'habitus' in his sociological studies?
options: The culture of increasing consumerisation of post-capitalist societies.
A person's posture, speech and the mental habit of perception, classification, appreciation, feeling and action.
The phenomenon of the masses succumbing to material fetishism of different types.
Personal habits that do not impact the society profoundly.
items.explanation: In Pierre Bourdieu's sociology (such as Outline of a Theory of Practice and Distinction), 'habitus' refers to the socially ingrained system of durable dispositions—including bodily posture, speech, and mental habits of perception, classification, appreciation, feeling, and action.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q23
items.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) are true about "Synecdoche" ?
(A) It is a comparison between two objects
(B) It is a figure of speech in which part refers to the whole
(C) It is a figure of speech in which the name of an attribute is substituted for that of the thing meant
(D) It is a comparison between two unrelated objects
(E) It is a figure of speech in which the whole refers to a part
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Synecdoche is a rhetorical trope in which a part stands for the whole (pars pro toto, B) or the whole stands for a part (totum pro parte, E), corresponding to Option 4: (B) and (E) Only.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q24
items.stem: Of the following characters in Jacobean plays, choose the one who is not a villainous character
options: Sir Giles Overreach (A New Way to Pay Old Debts)
items.explanation: While De Flores (The Changeling), Luke Frugal (The City Madam), and Sir Giles Overreach (A New Way to Pay Old Debts) are unrepentant villains, Daniel de Bosola in John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (1614) is a complex tragic malcontent who repents after the Duchess's murder and dies avenging her.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the sections of The Waste Land in the order in which they appear in the poem :
1. The Fire Sermon
2. Death by Water
3. A Game of Chess
4. What the Thunder Said
5. The Burial of the Dead
items.explanation: The five sections of T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) appear in the sequence: I. The Burial of the Dead (5), II. A Game of Chess (3), III. The Fire Sermon (1), IV. Death by Water (2), and V. What the Thunder Said (4).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q26
items.stem: Who among the following was NOT one of the original members of Johnson's Literary Club?
items.explanation: The Literary Club (known simply as 'The Club') was founded in London in 1764 by Samuel Johnson and Sir Joshua Reynolds, with Oliver Goldsmith, Edmund Burke, and Sir John Hawkins among its original nine members; John Dryden died in 1700, over six decades earlier.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q27
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Which of the following statements are valid for postcolonial theory and literature? (A) Abrogation, resistance and assertion form the basis of postcolonial thought. (B) Postcolonial theory defends binaries of Master and Slave, White and Black, and Coloniser and Colonised. (C) Weep Not, Child is the first novel in English by an East African Writer, Ngugi Wa Thiong'o. (D) Wide Sargasso Sea by Jean Rhys is based on the experiences of colonized African population. (E) Homi K. Bhabha, Edward W. Said and Gayatri Spivak are important postcolonial thinkers. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (A), (C), and (E) are valid: abrogation and appropriation are foundational postcolonial strategies (The Empire Writes Back); Ngugi wa Thiong'o's Weep Not, Child (1964) was the first published English novel by an East African writer; and Said, Bhabha, and Spivak are key postcolonial theorists. Statement (B) is false because postcolonial theory deconstructs colonial binaries, and (D) is false because Wide Sargasso Sea is set in the Caribbean (Jamaica and Dominica), not Africa.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q28
items.stem: Which of these authors is not a writer of African American slave narratives ?
items.explanation: Phillis Wheatley (c. 1753–1784) was a pioneering neoclassicist poet whose Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773) made her the first African American author of a published book of poetry, whereas Frederick Douglass, Solomon Northup, and Sojourner Truth are famous for their prose slave narratives.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q29
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true about Bhavabhuti's Uttararamacharita?
A. The time-space of the play is divided into two broad sections/acts.
B. The first act of the play deals only with the birth and childhood of Rama.
C. It is a play based on the Ramayana.
D. Its theme has been derived from the last canto of the Ramayana.
E. In the second act of the play, Sita takes refuge in the hermitage of the sage, Visvamitra.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Bhavabhuti's Sanskrit play Uttararamacharita ('The Later Story of Rama') is based on the Ramayana (C), derives its plot from the Uttara Kanda or last canto of the epic (D), and structures its dramatic time-space across two broad movements of separation and reunion (A). Act I depicts Rama and Sita viewing painted scrolls of their past rather than Rama's childhood, and Sita finds refuge in Valmiki's hermitage rather than Visvamitra's; thus A, C, D only.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q30
items.stem:
Material feminism studies inequality
in terms of
items.explanation: Materialist (or socialist/Marxist) feminism examines social inequality through the dual lens of both socioeconomic class (capitalist modes of production and labour) and gender (patriarchal structures), rather than isolating gender from material conditions.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q31
items.stem:
Identify the correctly matched group :
List – I
i. Where Angels Fear to Tread
ii. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
iii. The Plumed Serpent
iv. An Outcast of the Islands
v. Under Western Eyes

List – II
1. Malay
2. Russia
3. Italy
4. Mexico
5. Dublin

Codes : i ii iii iv v
items.explanation: E. M. Forster's Where Angels Fear to Tread is set in Italy (i-3); James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man is set in Dublin (ii-5); D. H. Lawrence's The Plumed Serpent is set in Mexico (iii-4); Joseph Conrad's An Outcast of the Islands is set in the Malay Archipelago (iv-1); and Conrad's Under Western Eyes concerns Russia and Russian exiles (v-2).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q32
items.stem: In New Criticism, the key term ‘tension’ is associated with :
items.explanation: In his influential essay 'Tension in Poetry' (1938), American New Critic Allen Tate defined 'tension' as the central criterion of poetic excellence, derived by synthesising the semantic extremes of 'extension' (literal denotation) and 'intension' (figurative connotation).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q33
items.stem:
Which two of the following works does Walter Pater regard as examples of "great art" in his
essay "Style"?

A. Iliad

B. The Divine Comedy

C. Les Miserables

D. Faust

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: At the close of his 1888 essay 'Style' (collected in Appreciations, 1889), Walter Pater distinguishes between 'good art' (formal perfection of expression) and 'great art' (which is dedicated to the noble enlargement of human sympathy and truth). Pater explicitly names Dante's The Divine Comedy, Milton's Paradise Lost, Victor Hugo's Les Misérables, and the English Bible as examples of 'great art'.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q34
items.stem: A close friend of Dickens objected to the original ending of Great Expectations in which Estella remarries and Pip remains single. Dickens accordingly revised to a more conventional ending which suggests that Pip and Estella will marry. Who was the friend ?
items.explanation: While historical records show that novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton persuaded Charles Dickens to replace the original somber ending of Great Expectations (1861) with a more hopeful reunion between Pip and Estella, Bulwer-Lytton was omitted from the options and the official UGC key selected Dickens's close friend and collaborator Wilkie Collins.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q35
items.stem:
What is the correct sequence of the following feminist texts?
(A) Sexual Politics
(B) A World of Difference
(C) The Female Imagination
(D) Thinking About Women
(E) A Room of One's Own
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: The chronological order of these feminist texts is Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929, E), Mary Ellmann's Thinking About Women (1968, D), Kate Millett's Sexual Politics (1970, A), Patricia Meyer Spacks's The Female Imagination (1975, C), and Barbara Johnson's A World of Difference (1987, B).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q36
items.stem:
Which narrative poem by Lord Tennyson presents the story of a fisherman turned merchant-
sailor who, after a shipwreck, is marooned on a desert island ?
items.explanation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson's narrative poem Enoch Arden (1864) tells the tragic story of fisherman-turned-merchant-sailor Enoch Arden, who is shipwrecked on a desert island for ten years and returns home to find his wife Annie remarried to his childhood friend Philip Ray.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: A pidgin is formed by two mutually unintelligible speech communities trying to communicate using the
most obvious features of each other's language.
Statement II: Notwithstanding the number of years a pidgin is spoken, it can never become the mother tongue of a
community.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
items.explanation: A pidgin arises as a simplified contact language between speech communities lacking a common tongue (Statement I is correct); however, when a pidgin is acquired by children as their native mother tongue, it develops into a creole (Statement II is incorrect).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q38
items.stem:
Name the dominant meter of the following quatrain :

The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,

The lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea,

The plowman homeward plods his weary way,

And leaves the world to darkness and to me
items.explanation: This opening quatrain of Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751) is written in heroic quatrains—four-line stanzas of iambic pentameter (five iambic feet per line) rhyming ABAB.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q39
items.stem:
Which among the following are written by Roland Barthes:
A. Allegories of Reading
B. Mythologies
C. The Pleasure of the Text
D. Some Versions of Pastoral
E. What is an Author?
Choose the correct option given below:
items.explanation: Mythologies (1957, B) and The Pleasure of the Text (1973, C) were written by French theorist Roland Barthes. Allegories of Reading (1979) is by Paul de Man, Some Versions of Pastoral (1935) is by William Empson, and 'What Is an Author?' (1969) is by Michel Foucault.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q40
items.stem: In the poem or invocation at the opening of Book 3, Paradise Lost, Milton asks for divine help in writing his epic. He states that he is in particular need of aid because he has what he considers to be a disability. What is it?
items.explanation: In the opening invocation to Book 3 of Paradise Lost (1667), John Milton laments his total blindness, which struck him in 1652, and prays for divine internal illumination so that he may see and declare things invisible to mortal sight.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q41
items.stem:
Match the following authors with their respective works with the help of the code given below :
List – I
I. Oliver Goldsmith
II. John Gay
III. Samuel Johnson
IV. Richard Sheridan

List – II
1. The Vanity of Human Wishes
2. The Vicar of Wakefield
3. She Stoops to Conquer
4. The Beggar's Opera

Code : I II III IV
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith wrote the novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766, I-2), John Gay wrote the ballad opera The Beggar's Opera (1728, II-4), and Samuel Johnson wrote the satirical poem The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749, III-1), making (B) 2 4 1 3 the only matching code.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q42
items.stem: Which of the following acts were not passed during the Victorian Era ?
options: The Married Women’s Property Rights Act
items.explanation: Factory Acts, custody-of-infants laws and the Married Women's Property Acts were passed in Victoria's reign. Women's suffrage was granted only in 1918, after the Victorian era.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q43
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Sharankumar Limbale argues that Dalit literature is unique because: (A) This brings out the Dalit reality which is liminal in time and space. (B) This has unique historical and ideological concerns. (C) This offers literary and cultural representations of marginalised and dispossessed people. (D) This brings out narratives and discourses of pity. (E) It uses disrespectful and offensive language towards revered figures. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Towards an Aesthetic of Dalit Literature (2004), Sharankumar Limbale asserts that Dalit literature is unique because it articulates the liminal lived reality of Dalits (A), addresses distinctive historical and ideological struggles against caste oppression (B), and gives voice to marginalized and dispossessed communities (C). It explicitly rejects patronizing upper-caste narratives of pity (making D false) and does not exist simply to use offensive language (making E false).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q44
items.stem: Which of the following citations of an article published in a journal is in the correct format according to MLA Handbook (9th Edition)?
options: 2016. Boggs, Colleen Glenney. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, pp. 149-66
"Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, P. 149-66.
Boggs, Colleen Glenney, American Periodicals. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, P. 149-66
Boggs, Colleen Glenney. "Public Reading and the Civil War Draft Lottery." American Periodicals, vol. 26, no. 2, 2016, pp. 149-66.
items.explanation: MLA 9 style gives the author's name first, then the article title in quotation marks, then the journal title in italics, then volume, number, year and pages (pp.). Only option 4 follows this order.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q45
items.stem:
Arrange the following plays in their chronological order :
(A) The Tempest
(B) All For Love
(C) Volpone
(D) The School for Scandal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Volpone (1606), The Tempest (1611), All for Love (1677), The School for Scandal (1777).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q46
items.stem:
Which character in Anton Chekhov's play, The Cherry Orchard, first suggests the selling
of the orchard ?
items.explanation: In Act I of Anton Chekhov's play The Cherry Orchard (1904), the wealthy merchant Yermolai Lopakhin—whose ancestors were serfs on the estate—first proposes that Madame Ranevskaya save her family from bankruptcy by cutting down the cherry orchard and leasing the land as summer cottages.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : For deconstructive critics how human beings read and interpret signs they receive will determine their modes of knowing and being, whether those signs come in the form of literary texts or bank statements.
Reason (R) : The fact of the matter is that human beings use signs to function in the world and are always likely to do so.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Drawn from Lois Tyson's Critical Theory Today on deconstruction, both (A) and (R) are true: because human beings inevitably rely on signs to function in the world (R), the ways in which they read and interpret those signs shape their modes of knowing and being (A).

items.title: Mock #05 · Q48
items.stem: Who is the author of the essay "Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism" (1985)?
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak wrote the influential postcolonial feminist essay 'Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism' (Critical Inquiry, 1985), analyzing Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q49
items.stem:
Which of the following two plays have been written by Arthur Miller?

A. They Too Arise
B. The Real Thing
C. Some Kind of Love Story
D. Tiny Alice
E. The Crying of Lot 49

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Arthur Miller wrote They Too Arise (1936, his first college play) and the one-act drama Some Kind of Love Story (1982). Tom Stoppard wrote The Real Thing, Edward Albee wrote Tiny Alice, and Thomas Pynchon wrote the novel The Crying of Lot 49.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q66
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions (46 to 50):

We need to begin by casting doubt on the legitimacy of the notion of literature. The mere fact that the word exists, or that an academic institution has been built around it, does not mean that the thing itself is self-evident.
Reasons—perfectly empirical ones, to begin with—are not hard to find. The full history of the word literature and its equivalents in all languages and all eras has yet to be written, but even a perfunctory look at the question makes it clear that the term has not been around for ever. In the European languages, the word literature in its current sense is quite recent: it dates back—just barely—to the nineteenth century. Might we be dealing with a historical phenomenon rather than an "eternal" one? Moreover, many languages (many African languages, for example) have no generic term covering all literary productions. To these initial observations we may add the fragmentation characteristic of literature today. Who dares specify what is literature and what is not, given the irreducible variety of the writing that tends to be attached to it, from vastly different perspectives?
The argument is not conclusive: a notion may legitimately exist even if there is no specific term in the lexicon for it. But we have been led to cast the first shadow of doubt over the "naturalness" of literature. A theoretical examination of the problem proves no more reassuring. Where do we come by the conviction that there is indeed such a thing as literature? From experience. We study "literary" works in school, then in college; we find the "literary" type of book in specialized stores; we are in the habit of referring to "literary" authors in everyday conversation. An entity called "literature" functions at the level of intersubjective and social relations; this much seems beyond question. Fine. But what have we proved? That in the broader system of a given society or culture, an identifiable element exists that is known by the label literature. Have we thereby demonstrated that all the particular products that take on the function of "literature" possess common characteristics, which we can identify with legitimacy? Not at all.

Question 47:
Literature is unsustainable because :...
options: we are unclear as to what it means.
we are unsure as to its message.
we are not persuaded that the claims made for it are allowable and acceptable.
we cannot prove that its definitions are the right and the only possible ones.
items.explanation: The author argues that simply because a social institution exists does not mean that all products labeled 'literature' possess demonstrable, legitimate common characteristics that justify universal claims.

From a silence, somewhere deep within...

The poem is most similar in style and form to-
items.explanation: The poem has no fixed rhyme, no regular metre and uneven line lengths, so it is written in open (free) verse. It is not a sonnet or an ode, and it was not written for a special occasion.

items.title: Mock #05 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:
I believe implicitly that the child is not born mischievous in the bad sense of the term. If parents would behave themselves whilst the child is growing, before it is born and after, it is a well-known fact that the child would instinctively obey the law of truth and the law of love...
And believe me, from my experience of hundreds I was going to say thousands – of children, I know that they have perhaps a finer sense of honour than you or I have. The greatest lessons of life, if we would but stoop and humble ourselves, we would learn not from grown-up learned men, but from the so-called ignorant children. Jesus never uttered a loftier or a grander truth than when he said that wisdom cometh out of the mouth of babes. I believe it. I have noticed it in my experience that if we would approach babes in humility and innocence, we would learn wisdom from them. I have learned this one lesson – that what is impossible with man is child's play with God and if we have faith in that Divinity which presides on the destiny of the meanest of His creation, I have no doubt that all things are possible and in that final hope, I believe and pass my time and endeavour to obey His will. If we are to reach real peace in this world and if we are to carry on a real war against war, we shall have to begin with children; and if they will grow up in their natural innocence, we won't have to struggle, we won't have to pass fruitless, idle resolutions, but we shall go from love to love and peace to peace, until at last all the corners of the world are covered with that peace and love for which, consciously or unconsciously, the whole world is hungering.

Which 'will of God' is the author referring to in the line, "I believe and pass my time and endeavour to obey His will"?
options: To turn towards children in humility and innocence to learn wisdom.
To have faith in the Divinity and follow the commandments blindly as laid down in the scriptures.
To believe and spend time praying and following rituals properly.
To stoop before the grown ups and the learned men for guidance.
items.explanation: In this passage (from Mahatma Gandhi's October 1931 speech at the Montessori Training College in London), the author precedes 'I believe and pass my time and endeavour to obey His will' by citing Jesus's teaching that wisdom comes out of the mouths of babes and urging adults to approach children in humility and innocence to learn wisdom.
